title: feat(consent): canonical request bodies, and witnesses built from them (#928)
body:
feat(consent): canonical request bodies, and witnesses built from them (#928)

Same shape as #925, applied to the last family that had unset optional members
going out through an inline `json!` plus a conditional insert each.

New `protocols::consent_management` carries canonical bodies for request,
decision, revoke, list, approver-set and approver-list, each with
`skip_serializing_if` on its optionals. The null census then sees them — it
walks structs under `protocols/`, and an inline map is invisible to it — and the
six witnesses are built from the producer's body rather than transcribed.

Teeth checked rather than assumed: reverting the skips on `ConsentRequestBody`
and `ConsentListBody` fails the sweep with `null is not of type "string"`. The
old fixtures set those members and so could not have caught it.

The witnesses are minimal on purpose. `consent/list` and `consent/approver-list`
are now bare `{}` — the unfiltered call — and request sets neither hint. A
witness that fills every member leaves nothing unset, which is exactly where
this defect class lives.

The count was also wrong and is now measured. #925's note said 21 witnesses
still transcribed; the real figure was 20 — arithmetic rather than a count. The
module states 14 now, counted from the table, and splits them into three
situations of which only one is unfinished work: 5 are consumer-only and owe
nothing, 8 are pass-throughs needing an API decision rather than a test change,
and `messaging/ping` is a single required `nonce` where a body struct would
guard nothing — this defect class lives in unset optionals, and ping has none.

The fold is therefore complete for every family that could exhibit the defect.

title: docs(approvals): document the ceremony, not just the rule that triggers it
body:
The approvals convergence documented the **trigger** — `docs/02-vta/approvals.md`
covers which tasks need a human and how to say so — and left the **ceremony**
undocumented. Nothing described what goes on the wire once a `requireConsent`
rule fires, so the facts that decide whether an operator can actually run DTTE
lived only in changelog fragments and source comments.

## New: `docs/02-vta/task-consent.md`

The DTTE reference. The wire (three URIs, one of them dispatched), the four
hardcoded timers, the two-digest design and why one is salted, the match-code
entropy reasoning, who may approve, what the approver is shown, the three
re-checks at consume, and the pending-vs-denied distinction that decides when a
client may re-submit.

It also writes down four things that were only discoverable by reading source:

- `pnm approvals` / `pnm policy` are **Trust-Task-only**. The SDK's REST arm is
  unimplemented and no `/policies` route exists, so a REST-transport client gets
  a **404** rather than a permission error — which reads as a broken deployment.
- `vta setup --from` **cannot** carry `[policy]`. `WizardInputs` is
  `deny_unknown_fields`, so a `[policy]` section is a hard parse error, and setup
  always emits `policy: Default::default()`.
- `pnm approvals list` / `explain` do **not** surface enforcement state. A
  satisfiable rule prints cleanly while nothing is gated.
- Pre-upgrade consent rules are **deleted, not orphaned** — first boot runs
  `remove_stale_config_consent_policy`.

The trust-tasks 0.4 `digestMultibase` hazard is promoted here too. It was
documented in a fragment that a release collates and buries, and it is a live
interop trap: a mismatched approver stack produces an approval that is given,
accepted by the human, and then silently never takes effect.

## Removed: `docs/vta-step-up-art-of-the-possible.html`

A forward-looking vision page for a model that no longer exists. Doubly stale:
its headline principle ("Delegated modes mean a different person or device must
sign off") described the mechanism #914 deleted, and its roadmap listed "M-of-N
quorum on one challenge" as *next* when consent has shipped it — with tighter
binding — for some time. Left in place it argues for the wrong design.

Replaced by `docs/02-vta/task-consent-infographic.html`, which keeps the format
and tells the accurate story: why payload-binding beats session-elevation, the
six-step ceremony, the timers as hard numbers, and an honest live-vs-gap
capability read rather than a roadmap.

## Corrections

- `approvals-convergence.md`'s status header still read *"partially landed …
  Still open: the trigger collapse"* — landed in #914, with the same file saying
  so two sections down. The `## Not yet landed` heading had also swallowed the
  fully-landed REST-gap narrative; the genuine deferrals now sit under
  `## Deferred` and the landed sequencing is its own section.
- `docs/README.md` never listed `approvals.md` at all — not in the task table,
  not in the Part II contents — nor `approvals-convergence.md` in Part V. All
  four pages are now indexed.
- `CLAUDE.md` gained an **Approvals + task consent (DTTE)** integration flow. It
  was the one wire-level flow with its own Trust Task family missing from that
  map, so an agent reading the file found the retired config shape nowhere
  contradicted.
- `vta-policy/src/consent.rs` now expands DTTE in its module header and points at
  the operator doc. The acronym appeared ~14 times in the workspace, all prose,
  and never in the subsystem it names.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p vta-policy` clean.
- `check-changelogs.sh` and `check-version-bumps.sh` both pass
  (`vta-policy` 0.2.1 → 0.2.2 for the module-doc change).
- No broken relative links introduced; the 14 the tree already carries are
  pre-existing and untouched.
- Infographic HTML parses with no unclosed tags.

title: feat(vtc-service): publish which transports a community offers, and whether they answer
body:
A community's DID document says how to reach it — but resolving a `did:webvh`
and matching service `type`s is a lot to ask of someone who just wants to know
whether they can connect, and it still cannot tell them whether the endpoint on
the other side is *answering*.

That gap is what let a VTC advertise `#tsp` while silently dropping every join
(#923). From outside, a working transport and a dead one looked identical.

## What this adds

`GET /v1/community/public-profile` (public, unauthenticated, already fetched by
the default landing page) now carries a `transports` array:

```json
"transports": [
  { "protocol": "tsp",     "advertised": true,  "serviceable": true,
    "endpoint": "did:webvh:QmTS3…:mediator" },
  { "protocol": "didcomm", "advertised": false, "serviceable": true },
  { "protocol": "rest",    "advertised": true,  "serviceable": true,
    "endpoint": "https://first.openvtc.net" }
]
```

The default landing page renders it as a **Transports** row:

```
Transports   TSP      reachable        did:webvh:QmTS3…:mediator
             DIDCOMM  supported, not advertised
             REST     reachable        https://first.openvtc.net
```

## Two facts, deliberately not one

| Field | Question |
|---|---|
| `advertised` | Does the DID document offer it, so a resolving client will find it? |
| `serviceable` | Can this VTC answer on it *right now* — protocol compiled in, mediator connection live? |

Reachable means both. **`advertised && !serviceable` is exactly the state that
broke the reference deployment**, and collapsing these into one "reachable"
boolean would hide it the same way the original defect did. The interesting
combinations each render distinctly:

- `advertised, !serviceable` → "advertised, not responding" — clients will
  choose this and get nothing;
- `!advertised, serviceable` → "supported, not advertised" — normal
  mid-rollout, nothing routes to it yet;
- empty array → **unknown** (the community's own DID did not resolve), never
  "offers nothing".

## Design decisions worth reviewing

**The DID document stays authoritative.** This is a *view* of it, resolved at
request time, published so connectivity can be validated without resolving the
DID by hand — never a second source of truth. A client selecting a transport
still matches on the document's service `type` (CLAUDE.md D9). If the two ever
disagree, the document wins and this field is what is wrong. Said in the type
docs, the route docs, and the operator guide, because it is the one way this
feature could do harm.

**Resolved, not read from config or the local mirror.** A document can gain a
service long after the VTC last wrote its own `did.jsonl` — which is precisely
what happened here (`#tsp` arrived at DID log version 3, post-mint). The
resolver caches, so the common case costs no network despite the endpoint being
unauthenticated.

**`serviceable` is re-falsifiable (R6.2).** Off `MessagingService::status()` —
the same source `/health/diagnostics` uses — so a dropped mediator connection
flips it back. A published "reachable" that could never go false again would be
worse than publishing nothing.

**Endpoint, not page.** Operators replace the public website
(`website.root_dir`), so a landing-page-only change would vanish for exactly the
real deployments worth checking. The endpoint survives, is machine-readable for
CI and monitoring, and any custom site can render it. `website-default` renders
it from the fetch it already makes — no extra request.

## Disclosure

Nothing here is new information. `advertised` and `endpoint` come straight out
of the DID document, which anyone can resolve; `serviceable` is discoverable by
simply attempting the transport.

Deliberately **excluded**: build feature flags, version strings, and the
operator-facing remediation text from `transport_capability::Finding` — that
text names `--features tsp` and rebuild commands on purpose, for `vtc status`
and the daemon log, and must not ride out on an unauthenticated endpoint.
Pinned by tests at both layers (`the_public_view_leaks_no_build_detail` on the
wire type, `public_profile_leaks_no_build_configuration` on the route).

## Verification

- `transport_capability` 22/22 — including the new view tests: preference
  ordering, all four advertised×serviceable combinations, mediator-loss
  flipping messaging unserviceable while REST stays true, camelCase wire shape
  (R3.1), and the no-leak assertion
- `community_profile` 17/17 — including unknown-vs-none and the route-level
  no-leak check
- `join_tsp` 3/3 — the new `the_public_profile_publishes_a_usable_connectivity_view`
  drives the endpoint against a **real running VTC** whose DID actually resolves
  to a document advertising both transports, so the populated view is proven
  end to end rather than only in unit tests
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --lib` 727 pass (the 4 `admin_ui` failures are the
  known `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` empty-embedded-dir artifact; CI builds the UI)
- clippy + fmt clean; `--no-default-features` builds; `node --check` on the page JS
- OpenAPI tests green — utoipa resolves the nested schema, no registration needed
- both release guards pass (0.11.56 → 0.11.57)

title: feat(device): canonical request bodies, and witnesses built from them
body:
The #888 fold, applied to `device/*`. Follows #924, which converted the one witness that already had a type to point at; this one creates the types.

## The problem with the old shape

```rust
let mut payload = json!({ "consumerKind": …, "displayName": … });
if let Some(p) = platform { payload["platform"] = json!(p); }
```

That is not *wrong* — the conditional insert is exactly what kept `null` off the wire. But it is **unguarded** and **untestable**, and both matter:

- **Unguarded.** The invariant lives in the shape of an `if let`, so nothing checks it. `vta-sdk`'s null census (#921) walks structs under `protocols/` and would have caught `keys/create` (#919) — it cannot see an inline map. The next person who reaches for a struct here, exactly as #888 did for `keys/create`, reintroduces the defect with nothing to stop them.
- **Untestable.** A conformance witness has no type to point at, so it hand-writes the JSON and stops tracking the producer the moment the producer changes.

## What this does

New `protocols::device_management` with canonical bodies for **register, heartbeat, disable, wipe, set-wake**, each carrying `skip_serializing_if` on its optionals. Both properties then fall out for free: the census enforces the invariant, and the five witnesses are **built** rather than transcribed.

## The conversion has teeth — checked, not assumed

Reverting the skips on `DeviceHeartbeatBody` fails the sweep:

```text
device/heartbeat/0.1: request fails its own payload schema:
payload failed schema validation: null is not of type "string";
null is not of type "integer"
```

The old fixture set both members, so it could never have caught that — the same trap that made #924's *first* webvh conversion pass vacuously. Worth stating because it's the easy mistake in this work: a witness can look converted and exercise nothing.

## The witnesses got smaller on purpose

The old fixtures set members no producer here sends — `keyCustody`, `attestation`, `pushPlatform`, `issuedAt`. A witness asserting members we never emit proves nothing about our wire form, and leaves almost nothing unset, which is precisely where this defect class lives.

Heartbeat is now a bare `{}` (the "still here" call); register sets neither optional.

Correspondingly, only what the client can actually send is modelled. `attestation` and `keyCustody` are in the schema but have no producer here, and **a field nothing sets is a claim the type should not make**.

## `device/list` is deliberately not folded

Like `vault/*`, it takes a caller-supplied `Value` filter object and the SDK is a pass-through. Giving it a type is an API change, not a test change. It stays a transcription, now recorded as one rather than lumped in with the rest.

## Running total

The module's per-family account is updated: **21** witnesses still transcribe (down from 26) — 5 consumer-only and correct as they stand, 7 (`consent/*` + `messaging/ping`) awaiting this same fold, 8 pass-throughs awaiting an API decision.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` — 787 passed
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk` — green, including the null census now covering the new bodies
- `cargo clippy -p vta-sdk -p vta-service --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo +1.95.0 check --workspace --locked` — green **against the committed tree**, and `git status` clean afterwards (#924 failed CI because a rebase left the committed `Cargo.lock` stale while local runs silently fixed the working tree)

title: test(trust-tasks): witness the producer, not a transcription of it
body:
Stacked on #923 — review that first; this PR's diff is the second commit. Based there rather than on main so the version bumps stay ordered (the #920/#921 collision).

## The problem

The conformance sweep (#857) checks a *witness* per task against that task's schema. **26 of its 70 witnesses build their request from a hand-written `json!` literal** rather than from the type the producer actually sends.

A transcription only proves someone can type valid JSON. It stops tracking the producer the moment the producer changes, and stays green while live traffic fails.

`vta/webvh/dids/update/1.0` is the worked example, and the reason to start there: **its witness was transcribed, and #895 shipped anyway** — every unset member went out as `null`, so `pnm did-mgmt dids edit --label x` could not run at all.

## The root cause was an API boundary

That family's request shape lives in `flatten_with_did` — body members flattened beside `did` — and that function was **private** to `vta-sdk`. From another crate the shape was literally unassertable except by hand-writing it, so the witness had no honest option.

`flatten_with_did` is now `pub` (re-exported as `vta_sdk::client::flatten_with_did`), and the witness is built by the producer's own shaping.

## The witness is deliberately a one-member update

`label` and nothing else — the invocation that could not run. A witness that set most members would leave almost nothing unset and so would not exercise the defect at all.

That distinction is not theoretical: **my first version of this conversion set five members, and passed happily with the fix reverted.** Only after narrowing it to one member did reverting a `skip_serializing_if` reproduce #895:

```text
vta/webvh/dids/update/1.0: request fails its own payload schema:
payload failed schema validation: null is not of type "integer"
```

## The remaining 25, documented accurately for the first time

The module claimed these were transcribed because "the slice's wire type is module-private (consent, task-consent, vault)". **That is no longer true — 21 of the 26 name a `vta-sdk` client method that exists today.** The honest position, now recorded per family:

| Family | Count | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `auth/{whoami,sessions-list,step-up/approve-response}`, `task-consent/decision` | 5 | VTA is the **consumer**; no producer of ours sends these. A fixture is the correct witness — no further work. |
| `consent/*`, `device/*`, `messaging/ping` | 13 | Producer exists but builds inline `json!` with a conditional insert per optional member. **No type to witness.** Needs the #888 canonical-body fold applied to these families first. |
| `vault/*` | 7 | SDK is a pass-through over a caller-supplied `Value`, contributing at most one member. No SDK type exists; inventing one is an API change, not a test change. |

So the outstanding work is **one producer fold plus one API decision** — materially smaller and better-shaped than "rewrite 26 fixtures", which is why it is written into the module rather than left as a count in an issue.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` — 787 passed
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk` — green
- `cargo clippy -p vta-sdk -p vta-service --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean
- Conversion verified non-vacuous by reverting a `skip_serializing_if` and confirming the sweep reproduces #895's exact error

title: fix(vtc-service): serve the TSP we advertise, and refuse to pretend otherwise
body:
A VTC whose DID document advertised `#tsp` (`TSPTransport`) and no
`DIDCommMessaging`, built without `--features tsp`, accepted every community
join and recorded none. The applicant saw a successful send; the operator saw

```
Error unpacking message: DidcommError("Cannot parse message as JSON",
"invalid number at line 1 column 2")
```

— an error naming neither TSP nor a missing feature.

## Root cause (confirmed in SDK source, not inferred)

`affinidi-messaging-sdk`'s websocket transport classifies TSP frames only under
its own `tsp` feature (`transports/websockets/websocket.rs:599`):

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "tsp")]      let force_packed = atm.tsp().is_tsp(&message);
#[cfg(not(feature = "tsp"))] let force_packed = false;
```

Without it the CESR frame is never tagged `Protocol::TSP`; it falls through to
`atm.unpack()` and dies at the `error!` on line 712. CESR qb64 begins with `-`,
which serde_json reads as the start of a number — hence "invalid number at line
1 column 2".

**Two cfg-gated warnings existed and neither could fire.** `vtc-service`'s
`Protocol::TSP` arm has a well-written "the `tsp` feature is disabled" warning,
and the SDK has its own in `tsp_to_inbound`'s fallback. The classification gate
above short-circuits both — the frame is never routed to either. The SDK's
comment on that arm reads *"A DIDComm-only build never advertises TSP, so this
is unreachable in practice."* Nothing enforced that assumption. This PR does.

## A correction to the original framing

**The VTC never minted `#tsp`.** The `vtc-host` template emits `#vtc-rest` and
`#vtc-status-list` only, and `vtc-service` has no service-management surface at
all. Reading the live log at `https://webvh.storm.ws/first-vtc/did.jsonl`:

| version | date | services |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-06-21 | `VTCRest`, `VTCStatusList` |
| 2 | 2026-07-22 | `VTCRest`, `VTCStatusList` |
| 3 | 2026-07-26 | `VTCRest`, `VTCStatusList`, **`TSPTransport`** |

`#tsp` was published *after* mint, externally. So "have the setup path refuse to
advertise `#tsp`" would have been a no-op, and any mint-time gate would have
passed the exact deployment that failed. The check has to run against the
document **as resolved**, at startup.

## What changed

- **`tsp` is now a default feature of `vtc-service`**, so the shipped binary
  serves what its document may advertise. Receive-side only — this is Phase A of
  `docs/05-design-notes/tsp-enablement.md` §12, *not* the Phase B flip.
  `handle_tsp` answers over TSP because the caller waits on that correlation;
  VTC-initiated `send_to_member` stays DIDComm (§14 Q4) and is untouched.
- **New `vtc-service/src/transport_capability.rs`** compares advertised
  transports against served ones, matching on service `type`, never on the
  `#id` fragment (D9). Two call sites:
  - `server::run` refuses to boot when the document the VTC itself publishes
    (local `did.jsonl`) advertises something unservable. Fail-closed on a
    *positive* determination only — a missing or unreadable log passes, so a
    stale mirror is never an outage.
  - `run_didcomm_service` re-checks the **resolved** document (the case above).
    Three-valued: `Ok`; `Degraded` — loud error but starts, so one unservable
    transport doesn't take down a working one; `Unreachable` — listener declines
    to start rather than hold a socket that drops every frame, REST keeps
    serving.
- **Errors name the failure class** (R6.4): which transport, why this build
  cannot serve it, and both remediations (rebuild with `--features tsp`, or
  remove the service entry). Asserted by test.
- **TSP-only is flagged.** Phase A is "advertise TSP **+** DIDComm". The
  template advertises neither by default, so a TSP-only document is what an
  operator gets by adding `#tsp` post-mint and never adding `#didcomm`, which
  strands every peer that doesn't speak TSP. Now warned at startup and written
  down in `tsp-enablement.md` §12.1.
- **The TSP receive path is exercised, not just compiled.**
  `MockVtcDidcomm::start_with_tsp` mints a VTC `did:peer` advertising both
  transports; `TestJoinClient::send_tsp` seals a real CESR frame through an
  embedded TSP-routing mediator; `tests/join_tsp.rs` asserts the join reaches
  `dispatch_trust_task_core` and is stored. New CI step runs it.

## Two traps worth flagging for review

**The negative-arm tests would have been vacuous.** `vtc-service`'s
`[dev-dependencies]` self-dep leaves `default-features` on, so Cargo unifies
defaults into *every* test build — `--no-default-features` silently reuses the
same binary (same hash, ~0.3s, runs the cfg-gated-on tests). A
`#[cfg(not(feature = "tsp"))]` unit test here can never compile in, never run,
and never fail. The predicates therefore take the served set as a **parameter**
(`TSP_BUILD` / `NON_TSP_BUILD`), with exactly one `cfg!`-reading function and a
test pinning it to the compiled feature. Verified non-vacuous by mutation:
widening `NON_TSP_BUILD` fails 5 of 10 tests.

**The embedded test mediator needed its own `tsp` feature.** Without it
`/inbound` doesn't understand `Content-Type: application/tsp` and parses the
CESR body as a DIDComm envelope, rejecting the send with
`400 w.m.message.deserialize` — the mediator-side twin of the same bug, whose
error also names DIDComm and never TSP. Note the mediator's `did:peer` *always*
advertises `#tsp` regardless of the feature, so a successful VID resolve is not
evidence TSP routing is on.

## Definition of done

| Requirement | Status |
|---|---|
| A join over TSP reaches the dispatcher and is recorded | `tests/join_tsp.rs`; verified `transport="tsp"` in the orchestrator log |
| Cannot advertise `#tsp` in a build that can't serve it — by test, not convention | 10 unit tests + boot gate + resolved-doc check |
| Inbound frame on an unsupported transport errors naming transport and reason | `UnservableTransport::remediation`, asserted |
| CI exercises the TSP receive path | new `features`-job step, real mediator + real CESR frame |

## Verification

- `join_tsp` 2/2, `join_didcomm` 3/3 (unchanged by the `start()` refactor)
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --lib` — 715 pass. The 4 `admin_ui::tests`
  failures are the known `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` empty-embedded-dir
  artifact; CI builds the UI, so they pass there.
- `cargo clippy --features didcomm-harness --all-targets` clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean
- `--no-default-features --features setup,keyring` builds; `cargo check --workspace` clean
- `check-version-bumps.sh` and `check-changelogs.sh` both pass (0.11.55 → 0.11.56)


---

## Update — all four document-vs-binary cases, plus `vtc status`

Second commit (`81380356`). The boot check originally only acted on the
unservable-transport case. `findings_against` is now the single source for every
relationship between what the document advertises and what the binary serves,
and the boot gate, the messaging listener and `vtc status` all render it — so an
operator who runs `vtc status` to explain a boot refusal gets the same story,
not a second one.

| Document vs binary | Severity | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Advertised but unservable | **Error** | refuses to boot; listener stops if nothing servable remains |
| No messaging service advertised at all | **Warn** | legal — exactly what `vtc-host` mints — but nothing reaches the VTC over a mediator |
| TSP advertised, no DIDComm behind it | **Warn** | no fallback for a peer that doesn't speak TSP |
| Served but not advertised | **Info** | normal staged rollout; never a fault |

That last row is deliberately informational: shipping the capable binary before
adding the service entry is the correct rollout order, and making it an error
would make that order unshippable.

**`vtc status` grows a `Transports` section** — what this build serves, what the
document advertises in preference order, and every finding. "Will it refuse if I
restart" is now answerable without restarting.

**`vta-sdk` 0.21.14** — the `vtc-host` template description pointed at
`docs/03-integrating/runtime-service-management.md`, a directory that does not
exist in the tree; corrected to `docs/02-vta/`. Also reworded: it claimed
*DIDComm* is not advertised by default, when in fact **no** messaging transport
is, and it now says to add both when adding either, with the reason. Patch bump,
so the `[patch.crates-io]` self-pin and every `"0.21"` dependent are unaffected.

### On the "name what it received" half

Worth being explicit, because it is the one item I could not fully close in this
repo. For **DIDComm v1** and **unknown protocols**, `vtc-service`'s dispatch loop
already warns by name. For **TSP without the feature**, the rejecting layer is
`affinidi-messaging-sdk`'s websocket transport — a dependency — and the frame
never reaches any `vtc-service` code, so no change here can make that specific
error name TSP. The two SDK-side warnings that *would* have named it are both
unreachable for the same reason (the outer classification gate short-circuits
the inner one).

So the mitigation is to make the condition impossible to run in rather than
better-reported once hit: `tsp` default-on, plus a boot gate that names it
before any frame arrives. Fixing the SDK's message is a genuine follow-up, but
it belongs in `affinidi-tdk-rs`, not here.

### Verification (both commits)

- `transport_capability` 15/15 — including the new no-messaging, staged-rollout
  and severity-ordering cases
- `join_tsp` 2/2, `join_didcomm` 3/3
- `cargo clippy --features didcomm-harness --all-targets` clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean
- `vta-sdk` `did_templates` 59/59 (template description is validated by
  `every_builtin_parses_and_validates`)
- `--no-default-features --features setup,keyring` builds; `cargo check --workspace` clean
- both release guards pass for both crates

title: feat(join): attribute the submit transport, and refuse an unreachable community
body:
A join that is never acknowledged used to say only:

> ⚠ no response from the community yet — the request may not have been received

That reads identically whether the community ignored the request, the mediator dropped it, or the community **could not decode the transport its own DID document advertises** — and only the last of those is fixed somewhere other than here. Telling them apart cost a night of log-reading against a VTC advertising `#tsp` that its binary could not speak.

## Not a transport fallback — deliberately

Falling back is the wrong answer twice over:

1. **This repo already removed one.** #207, the commit two before this branch, is *"reopen the bootstrap transport, don't fall back to REST"* — the fallback masked a working TSP path and produced a worse failure.
2. **It would not have helped.** That VTC advertises `#vtc-rest`, `#vtc-status-list`, `#tsp` and **no `DIDCommMessaging` service at all**. There was nothing to fall back to. "Works with any combination" cannot rescue a peer offering one broken transport.

And a client that papers over a peer advertising a transport it cannot serve guarantees the peer is never fixed, while every other client — the mobile agent, the PNM/CNM CLIs — carries the same workaround. TSP and DIDComm also differ in their authentication properties, so a silent downgrade changes the security posture without telling the user.

## What this does instead

**1. Record the transport.** `CommunityRecord` gains `submit_transport`, set by the join flow from the transport discovery it already performs. Written *absent, not null*, on records that predate it — the `skip_serializing_if` habit from VTI #919, which is this same defect class one layer down.

**2. Name it in the warning.**

> ⚠ no response from the community yet (sent over TSP) — the request may not have been received

R6.4: the operator can now tell the failure modes apart at a glance.

**3. Preflight before minting.** A community whose document advertises no messaging transport cannot be joined at all, and discovering that *after* the persona mint leaves an orphaned identity attached to a request nobody could receive. `peer_messaging_transports` answers both halves from the one resolve `resolve_vta_with_resolver` already performs, and the flow refuses before anything is created:

> This community advertises no messaging transport (…). Its DID document offers neither a TSP nor a DIDComm service, so a join request cannot reach it. Nothing was created.

## Scope boundary, pinned by a test

This checks what a document **offers**, not whether the peer can serve it — no client can know that before sending. A test asserts a TSP-only peer stays joinable, so nobody later "improves" this into the reachability probe (or the fallback) it declines to be.

## Also

`InboundTransport` → `MessagingTransport`, now serialisable: one type for the concept rather than a parallel enum for the outbound direction. The compiler covered the rename.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` — 16 test binaries, all green
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean
- New tests cover the preference order, the not-joinable case, and the TSP-only boundary above; the record test asserts the transport is carried

Not covered: nothing here makes a peer that advertises a transport it cannot serve work. That fix belongs in the VTC — its DID document should not advertise `#tsp` when built without the (non-default) `tsp` feature.

title: fix(logs): say what arrived, over which transport, and keep the record
body:
Five defects, all found while debugging a join that was **in fact succeeding**.

## The log named the version, not the task

The inbound summary took the last path segment of the type URI. A Trust Task URI *ends in its version*:

```
https://trusttasks.org/spec/credential-exchange/issue/0.1
                                                     ^^^ last segment
```

So every inbound message rendered as `Inbound: 0.1`. It went unnoticed because legacy DIDComm types end in the action (`…/trust-ping/2.0/ping` → `ping`) — the label only became useless once the stack moved to Trust Tasks, which is exactly when the log became worth reading.

New `display::task_label` keeps the part that identifies the task, so a VTC's membership credential now reads `credential-exchange/issue/0.1`.

## It claimed DIDComm for everything

The detail pane hardcoded `"Inbound DIDComm Message"`. The pump *knows* the transport — it matches on `Protocol` to decode the payload — but `DIDCommEvent::InboundMessage` dropped it before any consumer could see it, so the log guessed. It guessed wrong for every TSP frame, and TSP is the transport this stack prefers and the one the VTC advertises. The event now carries `InboundTransport`, and the existing DIDComm transport e2e asserts it.

## `OPENVTC_DEBUG_LOG` truncated on every launch

`File::create` meant the restart used to reproduce a failure destroyed the evidence from the run that failed — the exact workflow the variable exists to serve. Now appends, with a run banner so restarts stay visible within one file.

## A join left no durable trace

The ceremony's running commentary lives in `state.join` — transient UI, gone on the next launch. Nothing in the join or membership path wrote to the *persisted* log, because no family covered it. After a restart there was no record a join had been attempted at all.

Adds `LogFamily::Community` and writes two entries that survive: the submitted join, and the credential that admits you — distinguishing "membership is now Active" from a later credential by comparing status either side of the handler, so the log says what *changed* rather than that a message arrived.

## Retention raised to 200 — and the ceiling stopped being persisted

At 100, one busy session's inbound traffic could evict the community events that are the reason to keep a log at all.

Raising the default alone would not have worked. `limit` was a **serialized** field, so every config already on disk carried `"limit": 100` and would have kept using it. The raise would have silently applied only to users with no config yet — precisely the ones with no logs to lose — while passing every test written against a fresh `Default`.

Nothing ever sets `limit` but `Default`; it is policy, not user data. It is now `#[serde(skip)]` with an explicit `default_limit()`, so the ceiling comes from code on every load, and a stored `limit` in an older config is ignored (nothing here denies unknown fields) — no migration needed.

## Why this mattered

The middle two are what made the live debugging harder than it needed to be. The VTC **was** answering, with `credential-exchange/issue/0.1` — the membership credential — and the activity log rendered it as `Inbound: 0.1`, indistinguishable from anything else.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` — 16 test binaries, all green
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean
- Tests pin: the label behaviour including the version-suffix case that caused this and degenerate (peer-controlled) input; that an older config with `"limit": 100` loads at 200; and that `limit` is no longer written back out

title: fix(logs): say what arrived, over which transport, and keep the record (#209)
body:
fix(logs): say what arrived, over which transport, and keep the record (#209)

* fix(logs): say what arrived, over which transport, and keep the record

Four defects, all found while debugging a join that was in fact succeeding.

**The activity log named the version, not the task.** The inbound summary took
the last path segment of the type URI — but a Trust Task URI *ends in its
version*, so every inbound message rendered as `Inbound: 0.1`. It went
unnoticed because legacy DIDComm types end in the action
(`…/trust-ping/2.0/ping` → `ping`); the label only became useless once the
stack moved to Trust Tasks, which is exactly when the log became worth reading.
New `display::task_label` keeps the part that identifies the task, so a VTC's
membership credential now reads `credential-exchange/issue/0.1`.

**It claimed DIDComm for everything.** The detail pane hardcoded "Inbound
DIDComm Message". The pump *knows* the transport — it matches on `Protocol` to
decode the payload — but `DIDCommEvent::InboundMessage` dropped it, so the log
guessed, and guessed wrong for every TSP frame. TSP is the transport this stack
prefers and the one the VTC advertises, so the label was wrong precisely when
it mattered. The event now carries `InboundTransport` and the log reports it.

**`OPENVTC_DEBUG_LOG` truncated on every launch.** `File::create` meant the
restart used to reproduce a failure destroyed the evidence from the run that
failed — the exact workflow the variable exists to serve. Now appends, with a
run banner so restarts stay visible in one file.

**A join left no durable trace.** The ceremony's running commentary lives in
`state.join`, which is transient UI, and nothing in the join or membership path
wrote to the persisted log — there was no family for it. After a restart there
was no record that a join had been attempted at all. Adds
`LogFamily::Community` and writes two entries that survive: the submitted join,
and the credential that admits you (distinguishing "membership is now Active"
from a subsequent credential, by comparing status either side of the handler).

The last two are what made the live debugging harder than it needed to be: the
VTC *was* answering, with `credential-exchange/issue/0.1`, and the log rendered
that as `Inbound: 0.1`.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(logs): retain 200 entries, and stop persisting the ceiling

Raises the retained-entry limit 100 -> 200: at 100, one busy session's inbound
traffic could evict the community-lifecycle entries that are the reason to keep
a log at all.

Changing the default alone would not have done it. `limit` was a *serialized*
field, so every config already on disk carried `"limit": 100` and would have
gone on using it — the raise would have silently applied only to users with no
config yet, who are precisely the ones with no logs to lose, while passing
every test written against a fresh `Default`.

Nothing ever sets `limit` but `Default`; it is a policy constant, not user
data. So it is `#[serde(skip)]` with an explicit `default_limit()` now — the
ceiling comes from code on every load, and a stored `limit` in an older config
is ignored (nothing here denies unknown fields), so no migration is needed.

Two tests pin both halves: that an older config with `"limit": 100` loads at
200, and that the field is no longer written back out.

title: chore(release): vta-service 0.14.27 — 0.14.26 shipped without #921
body:
#920 and #921 both moved `vta-service` from 0.14.25 to **0.14.26**. Because they made the *same* edit to the same line, git merged the second one without a conflict and the bump silently disappeared — #921 landed on a version #920 had already published.

The publish workflow does not fail on that. It treats an already-published version as a no-op, and [the run went green](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/actions/runs/31459771492), so nothing said so.

**Result:** `vta-service 0.14.26` on crates.io is #920's tree, while main's 0.14.26 is #920 + #921.

The divergence is **dev-only** — a test file (`tests/producer_payload_conformance.rs`) and a dev-dependency feature; no library code differs. That is why this corrects forward cheaply rather than yanking: 0.14.27 republishes with the content main actually has, and the version-to-content invariant the release guards exist to protect holds again.

`vta-sdk` was unaffected — 0.21.13 published normally, since only #921 touched it.

Also corrects #921's changelog fragment, which still names 0.14.26.

## Worth noting

**Both release guards passed throughout.** `check-version-bumps.sh` asks whether a changed crate was bumped; `check-changelogs.sh` asks whether the bump is documented. Neither can see that the version being bumped *to* is already taken on crates.io — and two PRs in flight against the same crate is all it takes. If that is worth closing, the check is a `cargo info` / index lookup against the target version at CI time. Not done here; this PR is the correction, not the guard.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p vta-service` — clean
- Both release guards — pass (`0.14.26 -> 0.14.27`, documented)
- No source changes beyond the version string and the fragment heading

title: test(trust-tasks): check what we send, not what we wrote down
body:
Stacked on #919 — review that first; this PR's diff is the second commit.

#919 fixed `keys/create` sending `"mnemonic": null`. It did not answer the question the fix raised: **how many more are there, and what would have caught this?** Both defects of this shape (#895, #919) were found in production, by a person, from a rejected request. This adds the two checks that find them without one.

## A source census — `vta-sdk/tests/payload_null_census.rs`

Every `Option` member of every `Serialize` struct under `protocols/` must skip `None`, because every Trust Task schema types its optional members by what they hold and none accepts null. Exceptions go in `NULLABLE_BY_DESIGN` with a reason, checked in both directions so one cannot outlive the member it exempts.

Parsed with `syn`, not grepped — the attribute is routinely written across several lines, which a line-oriented regex misreads in exactly the direction that lets a violation through.

**Five latent violations on its first run**, all fixed here:

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `CreateAclResultBody::label` | also `SwapKeyResponseBody`, `UpdateAclResultBody`, `ChangeRoleResultBody` |
| `CreateContextResultBody::{did,description}` | |
| `CreateKeyResultBody::label` | the response half of the task #919 fixed |
| `SeedRecordBackup::retired_at` | its sibling `seed_enc` already skipped |
| `AclEntryBackup::label` | |

Each sits in a struct whose *sibling* members already skip — oversights, not decisions. Only `GetKeyResponseBody::key` is exempt, and that one is spec-mandated: `keys/show/0.1#response` types it `oneOf: [KeyRecord, null]` and requires it present, because "no such key" is a successful answer.

## A producer census — `vta-service/tests/producer_payload_conformance.rs`

The source census cannot see a payload built by hand, and the conformance sweep (#857) cannot see one at all — it checks a witness written in the test, and no client method runs during it.

So this drives the client methods themselves, through a new in-process transport (`vta_sdk::client::loopback`, behind `test-loopback`), with **every optional argument unset** — the shape that broke `keys/create` — and validates what they emit against the published schema. No VTA, no mediator, no socket: a unit test in cost, an integration test in what it covers.

**It found a live defect immediately.** `derive_and_sign_document` sent `"proofPurpose": null` on every call that did not name a purpose — and omitting the purpose is what selects the documented `assertionMethod` default, so *the documented way to call it was the way that could not work*.

#919 had already added `skip_serializing_if` to `DeriveAndSignDocumentBody`. The method never touched it, building a `json!` map instead. That is the gap between the two censuses in one example: fixing the struct does not fix a producer that does not use the struct. It now builds the canonical body, as #888 intended.

Four unvalidatable tasks are recorded in `UNPUBLISHED` with reasons. They share a pattern worth naming: every one is a legacy `vta/`-namespaced task the canonical folds have not reached, so **the unvalidatable surface is exactly the un-folded surface**, and each closes for free when its family is folded.

## On the loopback seam

It intercepts *ahead of* the transport rather than adding a `Transport` variant. A variant would have to be answered at each of the ~20 sites that match on `Transport`, almost all saying "unsupported" — twenty arms of noise in production code to serve a test seam. The hook touches the three functions that dispatch a Trust Task and leaves every transport match exhaustive over the transports that really exist.

## Not covered, deliberately

- **Framing** — TSP sealing, DIDComm authcrypt, mediator routing sit below the loopback point and still need a harness with a real mediator.
- **26 of the sweep's 70 witnesses** still transcribe their request as a `json!` fixture rather than building it from the producer. 21 of those name a client method that exists today, so the module comment calling those slices "module-private" is stale. Converting them is follow-up work.
- **Response-side validation** — `trust-tasks-rs` codegen emits `ValidatedPayload` for `Payload` but not `Response`, so there is still no embedded response schema to check against.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] `cargo check` passes for the entire workspace
- [x] `cargo test` passes (`vta-sdk` incl. the new census, `vta-service` lib 787, producer census 3)
- [x] `cargo fmt --check` clean
- [x] `cargo clippy --all-targets` clean on both touched crates
- [x] Both censuses verified non-vacuous — each was run against the un-fixed source and reproduced the exact production error
- [x] Changelog fragment `changelog.d/920-producer-payload-census.md`
- [x] Commits signed off (DCO)

title: [Proposal] Improve RAHP adoption with guided repository architecture, visual documentation, and specification pressure-testing workflow
body:
## Summary The RAHP repository is already developing into a strong and reusable risks-and-harms assurance toolkit. The main adoption barrier now appears to be **information architecture and discoverability**, rather than lack of substantive content. At present, a new contributor or standards author has to infer several important things: - which files define the portable RAHP method; - which files are the DTG-specific instance; - which files are canonical source data; - which outputs are generated; - how the artefacts relate to one another; - how RAHP should actually be used to pressure-test a specification; and - which findings belong in a specification versus governance, implementation guidance, runtime controls, or another layer. The repository would be easier to understand, adopt, and extend if it were reorganized around a **guided operating model**, supported by a small set of diagrams and a first-class specification pressure-testing workflow. This issue proposes an incremental path that should improve adoption without changing the underlying RAHP method unnecessarily. ## Relevance The current repository contains substantial value: - risks; - controls; - guardrails; - assurance tests; - metrics; - personas; - scenarios; - recommendations; - governance precedents; and - supporting tooling. The challenge is that the repository presently behaves more like a **collection of assurance artefacts** than a **guided method that another Working Group can immediately apply**. For adoption, the first questions a new user is likely to ask are: 1. What is RAHP? 2. How do I use it on my specification? 3. What is DTG-specific versus portable? 4. How do I contribute new findings? 5. How do findings map to changes in a specification? 6. What belongs outside the specification? The repository should make those answers obvious within the first few minutes. # 1. Align the repository layout with the architecture already implied by the documentation and tooling The README and contribution guidance describe a separation between: - `method/` - `data/` - `tools/` - `context/` - `build/` That separation is useful and should become the actual repository structure. The present archive still places canonical YAML, tooling, generated output, legacy documents, spreadsheets, and web artefacts close together. This makes it difficult for a newcomer to know what should be read, edited, generated, or ignored. ## Proposed repository structure ```text dtgwg-rahp-tf/ │ ├── README.md ├── QUICKSTART.md ├── ADOPTION.md ├── CONTRIBUTING.md ├── CHANGELOG.md ├── ROADMAP.md │ ├── docs/ │ ├── index.md │ ├── concepts.md │ ├── how-rahp-works.md │ ├── pressure-testing-a-spec.md │ ├── interpreting-results.md │ ├── governance-boundaries.md │ └── diagrams/ │ ├── repository-map.md │ ├── lifecycle.md │ └── artefact-relationships.md │ ├── method/ │ ├── lifecycle.yaml │ ├── vocabularies.yaml │ └── schema/ │ └── rahp.schema.json │ ├── data/ │ ├── instance.yaml │ ├── risks.yaml │ ├── controls.yaml │ ├── guardrails.yaml │ ├── assurance-tests.yaml │ ├── metrics.yaml │ ├── personas.yaml │ ├── user-stories.yaml │ ├── scenarios.yaml │ ├── epics.yaml │ ├── recommendations.yaml │ ├── risk-acceptances.yaml │ └── governance-precedents.yaml │ ├── examples/ │ ├── dtg-credential-spec/ │ │ ├── README.md │ │ └── pressure-test.md │ └── minimal-instance/ │ └── ... │ ├── tools/ │ ├── build.py │ ├── validate.py │ └── import_xlsx.py │ ├── context/ │ └── rahp.jsonld │ ├── build/ │ └── ... │ └── archive/ ├── legacy-spreadsheets/ └── legacy-documents/ ``` ## Why this helps This makes four distinctions immediately visible: - **method** = portable RAHP mechanics; - **data** = a concrete RAHP instance; - **tools** = validation/build automation; - **build** = generated output. The `examples/` directory then becomes the bridge between theory and use. # 2. Add a full repository map to the README A repository diagram would make the operating model understandable much faster than prose alone. The diagram should show meaning and information flow, not only folder names. ```mermaid flowchart TB USER["Standards WG / Spec Author / Reviewer"] subgraph METHOD["Portable RAHP Method"] LC["Lifecycle"] VOC["Controlled vocabularies"] SCH["Schemas & invariants"] end subgraph INSTANCE["RAHP Instance"] P["Personas"] US["User Stories"] SC["Scenarios"] RK["Risks"] CT["Controls"] GR["Guardrails"] AT["Assurance Tests"] M["Metrics"] REC["Recommendations"] RA["Risk Acceptances"] GP["Governance Precedents"] end subgraph TOOLING["Tooling"] VAL["Validator"] BUILD["Build system"] end subgraph OUTPUTS["Generated Views"] SITE["Human-readable site"] NORM["Standards action set"] JSON["JSON / JSON-LD"] MATRIX["Coverage & cross-reference views"] end SPEC["Target Specification"] USER --> METHOD METHOD --> INSTANCE SPEC --> P SPEC --> RK P --> US P --> SC US --> RK SC --> RK RK --> CT RK --> GR CT --> M GR --> AT RK --> REC CT --> REC GR --> REC RK --> RA RK --> GP INSTANCE --> VAL METHOD --> VAL INSTANCE --> BUILD METHOD --> BUILD VAL -->|"integrity / conformance"| INSTANCE BUILD --> SITE BUILD --> NORM BUILD --> JSON BUILD --> MATRIX REC --> SPEC ``` ## Core message conveyed by the diagram The intended mental model becomes: > **People and contexts surface scenarios; scenarios surface risks; risks drive controls and guardrails; guardrails become testable; findings feed back into specification development.** # 3. Make “pressure-testing a specification” a first-class RAHP workflow A strong use case for RAHP is not merely maintaining a risk register. It is using that risk corpus to pressure-test standards and specifications. ## Proposed workflow ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1. Select specification
or change set"] B["2. Establish affected
personas & contexts"] C["3. Test against existing
risk hypotheses"] D["4. Identify new or
changed harms"] E["5. Map controls,
guardrails & evidence"] F["6. Determine specification
vs governance boundary"] G["7. Produce actionable
recommendations"] H["8. Feed decisions back
into RAHP"] A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F --> G --> H H -. new evidence .-> C ``` ## Suggested documentation Add: ```text docs/pressure-testing-a-spec.md ``` This should explain: 1. how to select a target; 2. how to identify impacted personas and scenarios; 3. how to reuse existing RAHP risks before creating new ones; 4. how to identify harmful inferences or missing assurance semantics; 5. how to map findings to controls; 6. how to decide where remediation belongs; 7. how to record disposition; and 8. how to re-run the pressure test after a specification changes. # 4. Introduce a first-class “spec review / pressure test” record Pressure testing should ideally become reproducible and traceable. A minimal record could look like this: ```yaml review: id: SR-001 target: repository: trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec version: WD-01 commit: abc123 reviewed_against: rahp_version: v0.3 findings: - finding: F-001 risks: [RK-CR01, RK-CR02] disposition: specification status: open - finding: F-002 risks: [RK-SC02] disposition: resolved-by-pr reference: trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#12 ``` ## Why this is useful This would allow RAHP to track: - what was reviewed; - which RAHP version was used; - what risks were triggered; - what specification version was assessed; - whether findings remain open; - whether a PR or later revision resolves a finding; and - whether a future version should be re-tested. This moves RAHP from a static risk corpus toward **continuous standards assurance**. # 5. Add a disposition model so every finding has a control plane One of the most useful lessons from specification pressure testing is that a valid risk does **not** imply that its mitigation belongs in the specification being reviewed. RAHP should make that distinction explicit. ## Proposed controlled vocabulary ```text specification companion-specification governance implementation-guidance runtime-control operational-policy out-of-scope risk-accepted already-addressed resolved-by-pr ``` A finding should carry one of these dispositions. ## Why this matters Without a disposition model, standards authors may interpret RAHP as: > “Here are all the risks; put all the controls into the standard.” That would make RAHP harder to adopt. The better model is: > “Here is the risk. Now identify the correct control plane.” ## Suggested diagram ```mermaid flowchart TB R["RAHP finding"] Q{"Where must the
risk be controlled?"} S["Core specification"] C["Companion protocol
or binding"] G["Governance framework"] I["Implementation guidance"] O["Operational/runtime
control"] A["Formal risk acceptance"] R --> Q Q --> S Q --> C Q --> G Q --> I Q --> O Q --> A ``` This diagram could be placed in both the README and the specification pressure-testing guide. # 6. Add an artefact relationship diagram and concise glossary There are many RAHP artefact types. Their individual meanings are understandable, but their relationships are not immediately obvious to a first-time reader. A concise conceptual model would help. ## Suggested definitions | Artefact | Plain-language meaning | |---|---| | **Persona** | Who may be affected | | **User Story** | What that participant is trying to achieve | | **Scenario** | What happens in a concrete context | | **Risk** | What can go wrong | | **Harm** | Who bears the consequence and how | | **Control** | What reduces likelihood or impact | | **Guardrail** | What must be true before progression | | **Assurance Test** | How a guardrail or control is proven | | **Metric** | How behaviour is observed over time | | **Recommendation** | What should change | | **Risk Acceptance** | Where residual risk is consciously accepted | | **Governance Precedent** | Existing governance practice that informs treatment | ## Suggested relationship view ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Persona"] U["User Story"] S["Scenario"] R["Risk"] H["Harm"] C["Control"] G["Guardrail"] A["Assurance Test"] M["Metric"] REC["Recommendation"] P --> U P --> S U --> S S --> R R --> H R --> C R --> G G --> A C --> M R --> REC C --> REC G --> REC ``` This could become the conceptual spine of `docs/concepts.md`. # 7. Add a “minimum viable RAHP” adoption mode The existing corpus is rich. That is a strength for DTG, but it can also appear intimidating to another Working Group. A new adopter should not think that using RAHP requires populating every artefact class immediately. ## Proposed minimum viable assessment ```text 1 specification scope 3–6 relevant personas 5–15 risk hypotheses controls only where necessary guardrails only for hard-stop conditions recommendations as the primary output ``` The repository should explicitly say: > **You do not need to populate the entire RAHP model in order to use RAHP.** A small `examples/minimal-instance/` would make this concrete. # 8. Add an adoption guide The existing technical guidance is useful, but adoption would benefit from a short practical sequence. Suggested `ADOPTION.md`: ## Step 1 — Establish context Identify: - the specification or system; - expected participants; - decision points; - trust assumptions; - power asymmetries; and - known governance constraints. ## Step 2 — Reuse before inventing Search existing RAHP personas, scenarios, risks, and controls before creating new records. ## Step 3 — Pressure-test Ask: - what can go wrong? - who is harmed? - what harmful inference can an implementation make? - what remains cryptographically valid but governance-invalid? - what assumptions fail under adversarial or exceptional conditions? ## Step 4 — Determine the correct layer Decide whether the mitigation belongs in: - the core specification; - a companion protocol; - governance; - implementation guidance; - runtime controls; or - operational policy. ## Step 5 — Publish actionable findings For each finding, capture: - finding; - impact/harm; - affected persona; - relevant RAHP risks; - relevant controls/guardrails; - suggested resolution; - disposition; and - status. # 9. Change the README entry point from “repository contents” to “what do you want to do?” The README should offer task-oriented navigation before detailed architecture. For example: ## What do you want to do? ### Review a specification for risks and harms Start with: **Pressure-testing a specification** ### Understand the RAHP method Start with: **How RAHP works** ### Explore the current DTG findings Start with: **DTG RAHP instance** ### Adopt RAHP for another Working Group Start with: **Adoption guide** ### Contribute risks, controls, or evidence Start with: **Contributing** This would reduce the amount of repository knowledge a new user needs before taking a useful action. # 10. Give the generated site a guided narrative The generated views are useful, but they are primarily database-oriented. A more adoptable site could expose three top-level paths: ## Understand ```text Why RAHP → people and power → risks and harms → controls and guardrails → assurance ``` ## Apply ```text Choose specification → pressure test → analyse findings → determine control layer → publish recommendations ``` ## Explore ```text Personas → scenarios → risks → controls → metrics ``` The existing generated risk/control/matrix pages can remain exactly where they are, but become drill-down views rather than the primary entry point. # 11. Move legacy artefacts out of the primary navigation path Older spreadsheets, Word documents, and generated artefacts remain valuable for provenance and migration history. They should be retained, but moved under something like: ```text archive/ ├── legacy-spreadsheets/ ├── legacy-documents/ └── historical-builds/ ``` with a clear notice: > Historical artefacts. Do not edit. Current canonical RAHP data is maintained under `data/`. This would make the repository root substantially easier to read. # What this proposal is not trying to do This proposal does **not** suggest: - changing the underlying RAHP risk methodology; - adding large numbers of new risks or controls; - requiring every adopter to use the full DTG corpus; - moving governance requirements into technical specifications; or - making the repository more complicated. The objective is the opposite: **make the existing work easier to understand, apply, and adopt**. # Expected impact The main benefit would be a shift in how RAHP is perceived. Instead of appearing primarily as: > a structured risk and controls repository, it could be understood as: > **a repeatable assurance process for pressure-testing standards against risks and human harms, tracing findings to controls and evidence, and feeding actionable changes back into specification development.** That framing is closer to what the repository is already capable of doing. The combination of: 1. a repository architecture diagram; 2. an artefact relationship diagram; 3. a pressure-test workflow; 4. a disposition model; and 5. a worked DTG Credential Specification example would make that operating model much easier for Working Group members, specification authors, reviewers, and future adopters to understand.

title: fix(deps): vta-sdk 0.21.12 — key creation works over DIDComm and TSP again
body:
Joining a community died on its first round-trip:

```text
INFO: Joining did:webvh:QmXi1PZD4NEvcvjfErAzVoCGtBFEv7dhXZQJHvcFY4U83F:webvh.storm.ws:first-vtc…
INFO: Creating persona keys (signing, authentication, encryption)…
ERROR: Failed to create persona keys: Failed to create signing key: protocol error:
trust task failed [malformedRequest]: malformed request: payload does not conform to
https://trusttasks.org/spec/keys/create/0.1: payload failed schema validation:
null is not of type "string"

Join failed. Nothing was activated.
```

`CreateKeyBody` serialized its unset members as `null`, and `keys/create/0.1` types `mnemonic` / `label` / `contextId` as `"string"` — none of which accepts null. The VTA's payload-schema gate therefore refused **every** key creation that did not carry a BIP-39 phrase, which is every one this CLI makes. A join mints a persona's signing key before anything else, so it failed there and rolled back.

REST was unaffected: that leg serializes `CreateKeyRequest`, which already skipped its `None`s. Only the transports this CLI actually prefers were broken, which is why this surfaced now rather than earlier.

Nothing here had a lever over it — the payload is built inside the sdk's own `create_key`. Fixed upstream in **VTI #919** (vta-sdk 0.21.12 + vta-service 0.14.25); this is the floor bump that picks it up.

## Why a floor and not just a lockfile move

The `^0.21.11` requirement already admitted 0.21.12, so a `cargo update` alone would have fixed a working copy and left a clean checkout free to resolve back onto the broken release. The floor is the fix, same as the 0.21.11 (provisioning casing, VTI #917) and 0.21.10 (`trust-tasks-rs ^0.4` unification) floors above it. The dependency comment now records all three in order.

## Verification

- `cargo build --release` — resolves 0.21.12 from crates.io with a checksum, no `[patch]`
- `cargo test` — full workspace, all green
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features` — clean
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean

Not yet re-run against the live VTA; the join that produced the error above is the real check, and the same tree built with a local patch of the fix is what I have been testing with.

## Upstream follow-up

VTI #921 (stacked on #919) adds the two checks that would have caught this without a person hitting it: a source census over every wire type, and a producer census that drives the sdk's client methods with every optional argument unset and validates what they emit. The second found a further live defect on its first run.

title: test(vta-service): mediator-backed DIDComm + TSP transports for MockVta
body:
## What

Adds a `transport-harness` feature and `MockVta::start_with_transports`: an
embedded `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator`, a `did:peer:2` VTA identity
advertising `DIDCommMessaging` + `TSPTransport` at it, and the **production**
inbound loop (`messaging::service::run_inbound_loop`) — so a Trust Task
arriving on either transport reaches the same `dispatch_trust_task_core` spine
the REST route uses.

The REST-only `MockVta` cannot express this: the transport a client picks comes
from the VTA's DID *document*, and a `did:key` cannot carry a service block, so
against `start_provisionable` a client can only ever choose REST.

## Why `did:peer:2`

A `did:peer:2` encodes its services in the identifier, so it resolves offline
through the built-in `PeerResolver` **in the consumer's own resolver**, with
nothing seeded and no resolver-injection seam. That is the whole point: seeding
*this* mock's resolver would not help a caller in another process, which is the
trap VTI #813 already hit. The alternative needed `*_with_resolver` variants
threaded through `DIDCommSession`, `TspSession`, `VtaClient` and `SessionHub`,
because the VTA DID must resolve at pack/route time too, not just at discovery.

## The bug this took to get working

Every `DIDCacheClient` rejects a DID longer than `max_did_size_in_bytes`
(**default 1000**) in `resolve_document`, before any parsing. The two-service
`did:peer` was **1685 bytes** — both services embedded the mediator's own
540-byte DID, base64'd.

Neither side reports that as a size problem:

- **Our side**: auth retries 6× and fails the connect as a 30s
  `WebSocket isActive? command timed out`.
- **Mediator side**: resolving us for our sender key fails → `403 Forbidden`
  plus `authcrypt requires sender public key for decryption`, which reads like
  a key-id or secrets mismatch and says nothing about length.

**The message that names it is logged only by `affinidi_did_authentication`**
(the retry loop in `DIDAuthentication::authenticate`).
`affinidi_messaging_sdk=trace` and `affinidi_messaging_mediator=trace` both show
a clean challenge and then silence. Worth remembering for the next mediator-auth
mystery: put that target in `RUST_LOG` first.

Raising the limit is not available as a fix — the mediator builds its resolver
inside `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator`, which exposes no knob for it, and a
consumer in another process gets a stock resolver. So the DID has to fit:

- `#tsp` points at the mediator's **URL** rather than its DID. Under a
  1000-byte ceiling a two-service peer can embed a 540-byte mediator DID at most
  once — arithmetic, not preference.
- the DIDComm service drops its `accept` list (32 bytes).

That lands at **980 bytes**, asserted at mint time with the byte counts in the
failure message, so the next added service fails legibly instead of 30 seconds
later as a timeout.

### Scope of the `#tsp` deviation

Accepted deliberately and bounded to the harness. A production VTA is a
`did:webvh` — services live in the document, there is no size ceiling, and the
workspace convention (`#tsp`'s serviceEndpoint is the mediator's DID) holds
there unchanged. The comment at the call site says so. Note the mediator's *own*
DID already advertises `#tsp` as a URL, so both conventions are live in the
ecosystem; that skew is worth raising upstream independently of this PR.

## CI

`transport-harness` is not a default feature, so `cargo test --workspace` never
compiles any of this. Added an explicit step that **runs** the harness (embedded
mediator, real websocket handshake — a behaviour test, not a compile check),
beside the setup-wizard step that exists for the same reason.

## Also

Drops a `set_acl(ALLOW_ALL)` added while the failure was misread as a permission
problem — the account's default ACL is enough to connect and go live, verified
by deleting it and watching the test stay green.

## Testing

- `cargo test -p vta-service --features transport-harness transport_harness_tests` — 2 passed
- `cargo test -p vta-service` (the CI feature set) — green
- `cargo clippy -p vta-service --features transport-harness --all-targets` — clean

Both harness tests pass with **stock, default-configured resolvers everywhere**,
which is the property the harness exists to demonstrate.

title: test(vta-service): mediator-backed DIDComm + TSP transports for MockVta (#920)
body:
test(vta-service): mediator-backed DIDComm + TSP transports for MockVta (#920)

* wip(test-support): mediator-backed transports for MockVta

Incomplete — the websocket connect does not yet succeed. Committed so the
working parts and the failure state are not lost.

Adds a `transport-harness` feature and `MockVta::start_with_transports`:
an embedded `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator`, a `did:peer:2` VTA
identity advertising `DIDCommMessaging` + `TSPTransport` at it, and the
production `run_inbound_loop` so a Trust Task on either transport reaches
the same `dispatch_trust_task_core` spine REST uses.

did:peer:2 rather than a resolver-injection seam: the transport a client
picks comes from the VTA's DID *document*, and a did:key cannot carry a
service block, so against `start_provisionable` a client can only ever
choose REST. A did:peer encodes its services in the identifier, so it
resolves offline in the *consumer's* resolver with nothing seeded — which
is what VTI #813 showed is otherwise impossible across a process boundary.
The alternative needed `*_with_resolver` variants through DIDCommSession,
TspSession, VtaClient and SessionHub, because the VTA DID must resolve at
pack/route time too, not just at discovery.

Working: the option plumbing, the AppState transport slots (secrets
resolver, `#key-1`/`#key-2` vm ids, ATM, registered TSP profile), the
did:peer mint with both services, and shutdown ordering (loop → ATM
websocket → mediator; an abandoned ATM socket auto-reconnects for the rest
of the binary, vta-sdk #830).

Failing: `build_messaging` → `enable websocket: WebSocket isActive?
command timed out`. Not the ACL — registering the VTA as a local account
and setting ALLOW_ALL explicitly changes nothing (that fix is kept; the
default ACL genuinely is not enough).

Leading hypothesis, untested: the two-service did:peer. did:peer:2 numbers
multiple services `#service` / `#service-1`, and every working precedent
here (`TestVtaResponder`, `MockVtcDidcomm`, the mediator's own `add_user`)
mints a peer with exactly ONE DIDComm service. Next step is to drop the
TSPTransport entry and retry: if the socket then connects, the fault is
service numbering/selection, not the harness wiring.

The `#key-0` / `#sealed-transfer-0` keystore records are filed under
whatever DID is configured; those are record keys, not verification
methods resolved from the document, so the DID method is free. Confirmed
by the existing did:key mock, whose `#key-0` is likewise not a real VM.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* wip(test-support): isolate the failure to multi-service did:peer connect

Three experiments narrow the websocket timeout from the previous commit.
Still not working; the cause is now specific and upstream.

1. Drop the TSPTransport service → `build_messaging` SUCCEEDS. The
   listener connects, and the harness test gets all the way to its
   assertions, failing only on the now-absent TSP service. This also
   confirms the core premise: `["DIDCommMessaging"]` came back from a
   FOREIGN resolver, so did:peer offline discovery across a process
   boundary works exactly as intended.

2. Mint the two-service did:peer and resolve it with no mediator, no app
   and no websocket (`a_two_service_did_peer_encodes_both_transports`,
   kept) → PASSES. Types resolve as
   `["DIDCommMessaging", "TSPTransport"]` at `#service` / `#service-1`.
   So the identifier encodes both services correctly and the resolver
   reads them back. The encoding is not the problem.

3. Swap the order so TSPTransport is first → fails identically. So it is
   the PRESENCE of a second service, not its position, that breaks the
   connect. Neither `service.first()`-style selection nor DIDComm being
   shadowed explains it.

Conclusion: something in the DIDComm connect path — the ATM profile's
mediator resolution or the mediator's own account/routing lookup — cannot
handle a `did:peer` carrying more than one service, and fails as a
30s "isActive? command timed out" rather than as a resolution error.

Worth noting the asymmetry: the production VTA advertises `#tsp` AND
`#vta-didcomm` together and works — but on a `did:webvh`, whose service
ids are author-chosen rather than auto-numbered `#service` / `#service-1`.
Nothing in this repo mints a multi-service did:peer today; every existing
peer fixture (TestVtaResponder, MockVtcDidcomm, the test mediator's own
add_user) has exactly one DIDComm service. This is new ground, not a
regression.

Next step is to find where a DID document becomes a mediator endpoint in
the connect path and see what it does with two services — likely in
affinidi-messaging-sdk / affinidi-tdk rather than here. If that cannot be
fixed upstream cheaply, the fallback is the resolver-seam approach
originally scoped, which does not depend on did:peer at all.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* wip(test-support): debug logs name the real failure — auth, not endpoints

The '\''isActive? command timed out'\'' was a downstream symptom. With a
subscriber wired into the test, the actual error is:

  AuthenticationError("Authentication Aborted: Maximum number of
  authentication retries reached")

Mediator side, per attempt:
  authz: ACL found did_hash=9366fd80… acl="000000000007fffb"
  authenticate::challenge: Challenge sent to did:peer:2.Vz6MkpRN…

So the account exists, ALLOW_ALL is applied, and the mediator issues a
challenge. Then nothing further from the mediator, and the client opens a
fresh session and asks again — six times, then aborts. The failure is on
the challenge RESPONSE, after the client has the challenge in hand.

That rules out the endpoint-resolution theory from the previous commit.
The mediator'\''s own endpoints resolve correctly
(rest/ws http://127.0.0.1:PORT/mediator/v1), and the SDK'\''s
find_ws_endpoint iterates all services rather than taking the first, so
multi-service handling there was never the problem.

Worth recording: the mediator'\''s own DID advertises TSPTransport with a
URL ('\''s":"http://127.0.0.1:PORT/mediator/v1"'\''), while the VTA
convention vta-sdk'\''s resolve_vta reads is TSPTransport with a mediator
DID. Both conventions are live in the ecosystem, which is a contract skew
worth raising upstream regardless of how this harness resolves.

Next: instrument the client'\''s challenge-response step. Either packing the
response fails locally, or the mediator rejects it without logging at
debug. affinidi_messaging_sdk=trace did not show the send, so raising the
mediator to trace is the next cut.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(test-support): the did:peer was over the resolver's 1000-byte limit

The harness works. `MockVta::start_with_transports` now connects its
websocket, authenticates, goes live, and both transport tests pass — with
stock, default-configured resolvers everywhere.

One cause explains every symptom across the previous three commits. Every
`DIDCacheClient` rejects a DID longer than `max_did_size_in_bytes`
(default 1000) in `resolve_document`, before any parsing. The VTA's
two-service `did:peer` was **1685 bytes**, because both the DIDComm and
the TSP service embedded the mediator's own 540-byte DID, base64'd:

    10 (prefix) + 50 (V key) + 50 (E key) + 802 (didcomm svc) + 760 (tsp svc)

Neither side reports that as a size problem:

  * our own auth resolves the profile DID, fails the guard, and retries
    six times — surfacing as the 30s `WebSocket isActive? command timed
    out` from the first commit;
  * the mediator, resolving us for our sender key, answers the challenge
    response `403 Forbidden` and logs `authcrypt requires sender public
    key for decryption` — an error that reads like a key-id or secrets
    mismatch and says nothing about DID length.

The diagnosis took three commits because the error is invisible at the
log targets one reaches for. `affinidi_messaging_sdk=trace` and
`affinidi_messaging_mediator=trace` both show a clean challenge and then
silence; the actual message is logged by `affinidi_did_authentication`,
which neither target matches. That is the retry loop in
`DIDAuthentication::authenticate`, and it names the error exactly. Worth
remembering for the next mediator-auth mystery: **put
`affinidi_did_authentication` in `RUST_LOG` first.**

It also explains the earlier experiments without contradicting them.
Dropping TSPTransport worked because one service is 912 bytes, under the
limit with 88 to spare. Reordering failed identically because order does
not change length. And `a_two_service_did_peer_encodes_both_transports`
passed throughout — it points at a 21-byte fake mediator DID, so it was
never near the limit. The encoding was always fine; only the size was
not. Nothing about multi-service `did:peer` handling is broken upstream,
which retracts the previous commit's conclusion.

The fix is to make the DID fit, not to raise the limit. Raising it is not
available anyway: the mediator builds its resolver inside
`affinidi-messaging-test-mediator`, whose builder exposes no knob for it,
and a consumer in another process gets a stock resolver — which is the
offline resolvability this harness exists to demonstrate. So:

  * `#tsp` points at the mediator's URL rather than its DID. Under a
    1000-byte ceiling a two-service peer can embed a 540-byte mediator
    DID at most once; this is arithmetic, not preference. It deviates
    from the workspace convention (`#tsp`'s serviceEndpoint is the
    mediator's DID) but matches what this mediator advertises for its own
    `#tsp`, the contract skew the previous commit flagged. Flagged again
    here: it wants a decision, not a silent precedent.
  * the DIDComm service drops its `accept` list, worth 32 bytes.

That lands at 980 — 20 bytes of headroom, thin enough that the next
service or a longer mediator DID re-breaks it. So the size is asserted
where it is minted, with the byte counts in the message, instead of
re-emerging 30 seconds later as a timeout.

Also removes the `set_acl(ALLOW_ALL)` added while the failure was misread
as a permission problem. The account's default ACL is enough to connect
and go live — verified by deleting it and watching the test stay green.
`register_local_did` is kept.

Not yet done: `vta-service` is publishable and its version still matches
origin/main, so this needs a bump plus a `changelog.d/` fragment before
it can merge.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci(vta-service): run the transport harness, and claim 0.14.26

`transport-harness` is not a default feature, so `cargo test --workspace`
never compiles `MockVta::start_with_transports` — the harness whose whole
purpose is to let an *external* consumer drive a Trust Task over DIDComm
or TSP against the real dispatch spine. Left to the default job, a
refactor breaks it silently and the consumer finds out for us. It runs an
embedded mediator and a real websocket handshake, so it is a behaviour
test rather than a compile check: run it, don't just build it. Added
beside the setup-wizard step, which exists for the same reason.

Version: 0.14.25 is already claimed by #919, which is closer to merge, so
this branch takes 0.14.26.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(test-support): record the URL #tsp endpoint as a scoped decision

The deviation is accepted, and bounded to the harness: a production VTA is a did:webvh, whose services live in the document with no size ceiling, so the mediator-DID convention holds there unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(changelog): fragment for #920

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
